text: In 1861, Chicago lifted an entire hotel into the air... with the guests still inside.
tts: In eighteen sixty-one, Chicago lifted an entire hotel into the air... with the guests still inside.

text: Chicago was built on flat, swampy ground, barely above Lake Michigan. When it rained, the streets turned into deep, sucking mud.
Waste had nowhere to drain. And cholera struck the city again and again.
So engineer Ellis Chesbrough made a bold plan. Lay the sewers on top of the old streets, then bury them, raising the streets by up to fourteen feet.
But the buildings stayed where they were. Front doors now opened onto a wall of dirt.
The Tremont House, a grand brick hotel, was suddenly sinking below the new street. And its owners did not want to close.
So a young George Pullman and his partners brought in about five hundred men and five thousand jackscrews. On a signal, every man gave his screws a small turn. Then again. And again.
Inch by inch, the hotel rose about six feet. Inside, guests kept eating, sleeping, and checking in.
Chicago didn't just escape the mud. It lifted itself right out of it.
